en: From burning in the fire of love,
Only a spoonful of blood remains in her,
And her flesh is but a pale pulp.
Warrior Seytek, O leopard,
Know that she is deeply in love with you.
Her tiny soul cries out,
And she sobs in earnest;
Unable to reach you,
She is passing through a living death.
All the torments of this world
That hapless maiden now
Is enduring in these very days.
Therefore, Seytek,
Let us tire our horses and survey the land,
And ride out to meet her;
This year let us soothe her burning grief
And open the flower market of joy.
Let us ease the deep sorrow
Of Bermet, daughter of the peri.
Let ninety animals be slaughtered for her feast,
And let her name be proclaimed as Bermet.
Her spirit is exalted and her fame is great;
Look closely—she is a mighty blessing.
Among all humankind
No beauty like Bermet can be found.
My falcon blessed by Kydyr,
Every hardship has now been overcome;
Do not resist—heed my words.
Let us weary our horses over the distant road
And ride out to meet
The hapless peri-born maiden.
Let your valor become known;
Let the jealous foe rejoice bitterly at the news,
‘A peri bride has come to him!’
Quickly invoke Baabedin,
And in the name of your fierce father,
Dedicate a moon-hoofed horse,
So the people may rise in a thunderous celebration
And the great multitude may behold the spectacle.
Saddle your steed, valiant gray wolf;
God has granted aid with both hands”—
Thus Akjoltoy spoke,
Relating all the tidings.
As he was telling half
Of God’s true, life-giving message,
There stood his eleven companions,
And Baimyrza, son of Baitaylak—
Twelve thousand tigers,
Men of immeasurable swiftness.
He knew how to outwit the foe,
The best and cleverest strategist,
The one who tended the leopard hero,
And truly knew his innermost secrets;
When a grim enemy appeared,
He sent him tirelessly against the foe—
Ask no more of Baimyrza’s greatness.
He was the fierce hero’s companion,
His comrade even in death,
The one who rode out on reconnaissance,
And seized the hardest objectives;
If an enemy confronted him,
He brought devastation upon the foe.
Ask no more of the twelve heroes,
Külchoro’s chosen warriors,
Handsome men radiant as the sun;
Ask no more of their greatness.
When black muskets cracked,
They tirelessly attacked the foe
And entered the engulfing flames;
When fierce guns thundered,
They drove the enemy back without fear,
Wearing armor no bullet could pierce.
Every one of them
Struck the enemy with devastation.
They pitched the tents along the road.
Even if slaughter lasted six months,
These heroes never lost their wits;
Ask no more of those warriors.
At “Charge!” they spurred their horses;
At the slightest word they laid down terms.
Told to take a cap, they took a head;
Told to spill blood, they spilled an evil spirit;
Told to drink water, they drank poison.
When their righteous fury seized them,
They chased wild asses and turned them into cattle;
When their mounting rage seized them,
They laid the whole world waste.
They set grassy lands ablaze
And burned the meadows;
Whenever they seemed spent, they smoked anew,
Growing stronger from their very roots.
They poured blood into the dark waters,
Raising vast clouds of dust in battle,
Kicking at knucklebones and storming the khan’s court,
Throwing themselves wholly into such sport.
Where he stepped, Mount Küdür seemed to rise;
Whatever he stalked became his enemy.
The fierce leopard Seytek
Appeared magnificent as a lofty mountain.
In those days no mortal
Could approach Talas to face him.
He had barred every perilous road;
The Black Chinese and the countless Manchus
Stayed huddled within Kakhan, never venturing out,
For none possessed such courage.
All the heroes gathered,
And the enemy’s path was blocked;
No foe raided their pastures,
And no confronting enemy survived.
Once, amid the vast world,
While his fortune still stood secure,
Within the fortress with gates of steel,
In Kanykei’s stronghold,
Five stout palaces had been built—
Such was their heroic magnificence.
Many monuments of them remained in the world,
Including a separate palace
For Buurul, mighty as a camel stallion.
This splendid palace—
Seen from outside, it looked like one palace;
Once inside, it seemed a thousand palaces,
So vast was its magnificence.
It was cast and sculpted as though molded,
And its door was of white tin.
There were six stewards who tended the horses;
Baimyrza and Akjoltoy,
Whenever Seytek had need,
Were keen-witted men who found a solution.
When Akjoltoy had spoken thus,
All the heroes grew excited
And every warrior became animated.
They played chess and won from one another,
And drank kumis from the leather vat;
When they heard the news of the maiden,
They grew merry on kumis,
Until sweat streamed from their brows,
And they burst into clamor.
They drank spirits from horn cups
And joined the celebration.
Then the lions gave themselves
To unending merriment
And plunged into the revelry.
“The one God has freely
Granted us our desire,” they said;
“To Seytek, blessed by Kydyr,
A beauty from the peri folk has come,” they said.
A roaring tumult arose,
And that day the clamor burst forth.
“A beauty has unexpectedly come to him,” they said;
“This Seytek’s fortune
Surpasses that of his father Semetey,” they said.
The reason it surpassed his father’s was this:
His father, the fierce Semetey,
Had won Aichürök,
But suffered anguish and battled enemies;
His ancient foes attacked,
And his head was pledged to death.
The two giants, Chynkojo and Toltoy,
Brought about a terrible slaughter.
When his father took Chürök,
He plunged the people into suffering.
But for Seytek, whose fortune was greater,
The hapless daughter of the peri
Came of her own accord,
Without galling a single steed
Or causing pain to any soul.
When God wills, He grants;
The Night of Destiny has come to us.
The people rejoiced and the nation surged,
Swiftly invoking Baabedin;
In the name of magnanimous Manas,
They dedicated a moon-hoofed horse
And spoke many splendid blessings.
The noble hero, until then unmoved,
Ordered joyous games to begin
And had brought forth a white mare
That had borne no foal for six years.
When the mare was brought,
That noble hero, proud as a rooster,
Grasped both its ears and forelock
Together in his hands.
Without binding the mare’s legs,
He cut off its head.
He sacrificed it to the spirit
Of his grandfather Manas.
When the young man sacrificed the mare,
All the companions of the tiger’s heir
Cried out together:
“O noble leopard Manas,
May your spirit uphold us!”
All his comrades shouted,
“What a boundless deed!”
Every hero grew inspired,
Every swift, armed young horseman
Was filled with exultation:
“If only such good fortune came
To a mortal son like me,” they said;
“If only the one God
Granted a man his heart’s desire in this way,
What regret could remain in a young man?
If, by a man’s good fortune,
Such a peri beauty came to him,” they said.
The people’s cries gradually subsided,
And the crowd grew calm and quiet.
Into the echoing palace
The young men came running,
Throwing themselves into saddling the horse.
The leopard Seytek’s fierce nature
And heroic spirit became manifest,
While the immeasurably swift
Attendants rushed in every direction.
A white halter made by a maid,
A halter fitted to Kulansur,
A white halter tied with rounded knots,
Fitted for the mighty stallion—
They fastened it upon Kulansur.
An impenetrable pure-white caparison
They draped with fluttering skirts
Across the prancing thoroughbred.
Steel shoes with silver nails
They hammered onto his hooves.
They saddled him magnificently,
Striking awe into everyone who saw;
A leather saddlecloth and blue saddle pad
They placed upon the thoroughbred.
They had brought from the palace
The white saddle inherited
From Almambet of old.
Calling it a legacy of the noble hero,
They filled the people’s hearts with wonder.
The reason their hearts were satisfied—
If you ask about that saddle—
Forty craftsmen and Bölökbai
Had fitted it without the slightest flaw,
Assembling it piece by tiny piece.
When its value became known,
Many khans asked for it.
It was never given to those who asked;
Far from giving away the saddle,
They never let an impure man ride it.
Its front bow was of white gold,
And its rear bow of yellow gold.
So that it might shine on moonless nights
And delight the heart of its rider,
They had every part of the saddle
Ornately carved.
Upon its front and rear bows
They had rubies and precious jewels
Set in clusters the size of bowls.
The white saddle was of matchless beauty
And satisfied the heart of everyone who saw it.
The winged tulpar Kulansur
Filled all the people with awe.
They saddled the moon-browed Kulansur
With the golden saddle,
Moving with immeasurable speed.
